signals.title: A Local Search Agent Can Shrink the Context Tax of Coding Assistants · Hugging Face Blog
signals.excerpt:
ColGrep-Agent-2B moves repository exploration to a small local model. Its reported benchmark highlights a useful design pattern—and the accuracy, latency and evaluation questions teams should examine before adopting it.
...
Delegating repository exploration to a local specialist can compress context, but teams should validate retrieval coverage, end-to-end accuracy, latency and total compute on their own codebases.

Coding assistants do not spend all their tokens writing code. A substantial share can disappear into repository navigation: searching for an unfamiliar concept, opening likely files, tracing references and then carrying those observations through later turns. LightOn's ColGrep-Agent-2B release targets that exploration loop with a small model running beside the developer's main coding agent. The important idea is broader than one tool: expensive reasoning models do not necessarily need to perform every retrieval step themselves.

The release describes a 2-billion-parameter local agent layered on ColGrep's semantic code search. It can search, read files and return paths, line ranges and relevant code to a larger coding assistant. In the authors' evaluation, Claude Code handled 52 code-search questions across 13 repositories, with three runs in four search configurations. The fully delegated setup reportedly used 34.3% fewer API tokens than built-in grep, while observed correct-answer rates were 80.8% and 83.3% respectively. The authors correctly note that the accuracy difference was not statistically significant, but its confidence interval was wide enough to include a meaningful decline. These are code-location questions, not complete software-engineering tasks.
...
A specialized search agent changes the interface. Instead of exposing every exploratory step, it accepts a behavior-level question and returns a compact evidence bundle. If that bundle contains the right locations and enough surrounding code, the main agent can start reasoning from evidence rather than from a blank map. The savings therefore come from context compression as much as from better retrieval. Compute has not vanished; some of it has moved to a local model whose tokens are outside the hosted model's billing and context loop.

That distinction matters when comparing systems. A lower API-token count is not automatically lower total cost. Teams should also count local inference time, memory, index maintenance, installation overhead and the cost of bad retrieval. Privacy can improve because repository exploration stays local, but only if the entire indexing and inference path is operated as expected.
...
The evaluation offers a useful controlled comparison because the question and repository remain fixed while the search interface changes. Repeated runs and question-level confidence intervals are stronger evidence than a handful of favorable demonstrations. The reported “Balanced” configuration is especially informative: it matched grep's observed accuracy while saving 21.2% of tokens, suggesting that routing may be more robust than delegating every search.
...
The latency tradeoff is visible too. The delegated agent used fewer main-model turns but took longer per question in the reported aggregate. That may be acceptable for unattended work or costly hosted inference, and less attractive during rapid interactive debugging. Averages can also hide hardware sensitivity because local model speed depends on the available backend and memory.
...
Teams considering this pattern should assemble questions from their own completed issues rather than starting with synthetic prompts. Each question should name the user-visible behavior without revealing internal identifiers. Record the files and symbols a maintainer needed, then compare three modes: existing search tools, delegated semantic search and a hybrid router.

Score more than whether one expected file appears. Useful retrieval should cover every required location, avoid irrelevant context and provide enough neighboring code to support the next decision. Measure main-model input and output tokens, wall-clock time, local resource use and end-to-end task success. Review failures by type: missing an alias, stopping at an interface, overlooking configuration, or returning plausible but unrelated code. Those categories reveal whether tuning the index, prompt or routing policy is likely to help.

A safe rollout also preserves an escape hatch. The main agent should be able to fall back to literal search and direct file reads when delegated results are sparse or contradictory. For high-impact changes, returned line ranges are leads, not proof; the coding agent still needs to inspect current code, callers and tests. Read-only search permissions are a sensible default because a retrieval specialist does not need authority to modify the repository.
...
ColGrep-Agent-2B illustrates a modular agent architecture: assign a narrow, tool-heavy subproblem to a smaller local model and pass a compact result to the more capable model. The value depends less on parameter count than on a clean contract between the two layers. The specialist must return evidence that is concise, inspectable and easy to verify.

For coding tools, that contract can reduce repeated exploration without pretending retrieval is solved. The most credible adoption path is therefore incremental: benchmark on local questions, use hybrid routing, watch both accuracy and latency, and retain conventional search as a fallback. Token savings are valuable, but the real objective is reliable evidence per unit of time and compute.

signals.title: LLM Quantization Without Calibration Data Matches SmoothQuant: DualQuant Targets FP4 Hardware
signals.excerpt:
A new post-training quantization framework eliminates the calibration dataset long required to deploy large language models at 4-bit precision — and it does so at a moment when hardware support for FP4 inference is converging across three major accelerator lines at once.

The method, called DualQuant, was posted to arXiv on October 9 by researchers affiliated with d-Matrix, a Santa Clara AI inference chip startup. The framework targets the same W4A4 inference problem as SmoothQuant — compressing both weights and activations to 4-bit precision simultaneously — but requires no representative input data at quantization time. On a real packed W4A4 inference path for Llama-3.1-8B running on an RTX 4090, DualQuant delivered 2.61x memory reduction benchmark results and up to 2.46x throughput speedup over a BF16 baseline while matching SmoothQuant's accuracy. The news comes as the Open Compute Project's annual Global Summit — the standards-setting body for the MXFP4 format that DualQuant targets — runs this week in San Jose.
...
The Open Compute Project Global Summit runs October 12–15, 2026, in San Jose, and it is the institutional home of the Microscaling (MX) format standard — the open specification that defines MXFP4, the 4-bit block floating-point format now supported by AMD's Instinct MI350 series and Intel's forthcoming Xe3P data center GPU. NVIDIA's competing 4-bit format, NVFP4, is natively implemented in Blackwell NVFP4 Tensor Core specs that power the B100, B200, and GB200 series.

Both formats are already in active production deployment. NVIDIA has published NVFP4 checkpoints for DeepSeek models including V3.2 and V4, with DeepSeek V4 Blackwell NVFP4 performance reaching approximately 3,500 tokens per second on Blackwell hardware. AMD's MI355X surpassed one million tokens per second in MLPerf Inference 6.0. Intel's Xe3P architecture — detailed at Hot Chips 2026 in August — supports FP4 and MX microscaling with 480GB of LPDDR5X memory.
...
SmoothQuant (MIT/NVIDIA), the state of the art, addressed this by offline-migrating quantization difficulty from activations to weights via a per-channel scaling transformation. The transformation is computed from a small representative calibration sample — typically 512 to 2,048 input sequences run through the model before deployment. The approach works well enough that it has been incorporated into SmoothQuant TensorRT-LLM production integration and Amazon SageMaker. But it carries a hidden operational cost: for every new model variant, fine-tune, or deployment context, operators must maintain a curated calibration dataset, manage its versioning, and accept the risk that a dataset tuned to one distribution may subtly distort accuracy in another.
...
Research presented at ICLR 2026 established that MXFP4's power-of-two block scaling severely degrades accuracy in a way that prior calibration-based methods were not designed to address. MXFP4 uses 32-element blocks with a shared scale encoded in E8M0 format — meaning the shared exponent is rounded to a power of two. This is intentionally cheaper to implement in hardware — the OCP MX standard achieves roughly 12% relative area savings in tensor cores compared to NVFP4 — but it introduces additional quantization error that simple scaling strategies cannot recover from.

NVFP4, NVIDIA's proprietary format used in Blackwell Tensor Cores, uses 16-element blocks with an E4M3 shared scale that requires a real floating-point multiply — costlier in hardware but more accurate. The two formats are built on different block structures with different scale granularities, and prior dual-scaling methods including SmoothQuant were designed around tensor-level or per-channel quantization schemes that do not map cleanly onto either.

DualQuant's formulation parameterizes the weight-reconstruction problem to match each target format's specific block structure. The authors claim it is the DualQuant first MX NVFP4 method — the first dual-scaling method to formally support both the full MX family and NVIDIA's NVFP4.
...
The researchers evaluated DualQuant across Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, and Mixtral-8x7B on standard DualQuant benchmark evaluation results, including WikiText-2 perplexity, C4 perplexity, and zero-shot downstream tasks. Across most models and formats, DualQuant matched or exceeded SmoothQuant's accuracy despite having no access to calibration data, and it substantially outperformed other calibration-free baselines. The largest accuracy gains appear specifically on MX and NV block formats — consistent with the claim that the algorithm's format-native formulation gives it an advantage precisely where prior methods were not designed for the block structure.

The hardware validation on the RTX 4090 Ada Lovelace specs delivered 2.61x memory reduction and 2.46x throughput. A clarification is warranted for practitioners targeting Blackwell or AMD MI350: the RTX 4090 is an Ada Lovelace–architecture GPU (2022) that lacks hardware-native FP4 Tensor Cores. The benchmark implements a custom packed W4A4 integer kernel that packs 4-bit values into 8-bit or 16-bit registers — a genuine 4-bit computation path, but via integer packing rather than the E2M1 or E4M3 Tensor Core instructions that Blackwell and MI350 hardware execute. The accuracy parity between this real kernel and the paper's simulated ("fake") quantization results is meaningful — it confirms the algorithm works in hardware — but practitioners should be aware that throughput benchmarks on Blackwell or MI350 with native FP4 Tensor Cores were not reported in the paper. Those results, when they come, may differ.
...
A calibration-free method collapses this to a single offline computation on model weights alone — no dataset, no environment-specific tuning, no versioning. That simplification matters most for teams deploying models that are frequently fine-tuned (where recalibrating after every fine-tune is expensive), for domains where representative input data is proprietary or scarce, and for any workflow targeting multiple hardware backends at once, since DualQuant's single algorithm covers both MXFP4 and NVFP4 targets simultaneously.
...

...
MXFP4 is an open standard defined by the Open Compute Project's Microscaling (MX) specification, supported by AMD, Intel, Qualcomm, Microsoft, and others. It uses 32-element blocks with a power-of-two shared exponent (E8M0), which is efficient to implement in hardware but introduces more quantization error than alternatives. NVFP4 is NVIDIA's proprietary variant used in Blackwell Tensor Cores; it uses 16-element blocks with an E4M3 shared scale that requires a real multiply and achieves higher accuracy at slightly higher hardware cost. DualQuant is the first dual-scaling method formally designed to cover both.
...
With well-designed quantization, the accuracy hit at W4A4 precision can be made small. DualQuant's paper reports matching SmoothQuant — the calibration-based state of the art — on most tested models including Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, and Mixtral-8x7B, while substantially outperforming calibration-free baselines. Research from Meta presented at ICML 2026 found that naively applied MXFP4 quantization degrades accuracy by around 10% on average relative to BF16 baselines; DualQuant's format-native formulation is designed specifically to address that gap.
...
NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs (B100, B200, GB200) support NVFP4 natively in their Tensor Cores. AMD Instinct MI350 series (CDNA4 architecture) supports MXFP4 natively. Intel Xe3P (Crescent Island), detailed at Hot Chips 2026, supports both FP4 and MX microscaling. The RTX 4090 benchmark in DualQuant's paper uses a custom integer-packing kernel rather than hardware-native FP4 Tensor Cores, as Ada Lovelace predates FP4 Tensor Core support.

signals.excerpt:
MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post, we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators.

In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model — Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters — right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1), well above average human reading speed.
...
We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio, using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post. We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads.

We evaluate three frontier-class models (Table 1) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts — and thus parameters — active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively).
...
Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with `mlx_lm.benchmark`. For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line:
...
While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers.
...
Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the model’s inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the model’s layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes.
...
MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the MLX distributed documentation. These rely on fast inter-machine communication: macOS 26.2 introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives (`jaccl`, pronounced “jackal”) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that `jaccl` uses. Once the hosts are set up, MLX provides `mlx.launch`, a helper command to launch jobs across multiple nodes:
...
In this command, `--backend jaccl` specifies the RDMA Thunderbolt driver backend. Training frontier models within a compute budget requires co-designing models and infrastructure for both evaluation quality and computational efficiency. We use an efficiency gain (EG) metric to help guide our decisions: the ratio of compute required by a candidate to reach the same evaluation loss as the baseline. Compute can be measured in FLOPs (EG FLOPs) or in wall-clock time (EG time), and the two are complementary. We rely mainly on EG time, since it reflects the current state of our infrastructure. These optimizations enable us to train sparser models without significantly degrading MFU.

The announcement follows AMD's earlier release of the MI300X GPU, which was framed as a significant step in accelerating AI workloads. signals.excerpt:
# ModelScope’s EntroPack Lets 80GB Models Squeeze Onto 24GB GPUs

 By Bibhu Pattnaik October 14, 2026 October 14, 2026 

 

GPU memory compression got a new open-source tool Wednesday when ModelScope released EntroPack, a PyTorch library that lets developers tune how AI model weights are stored to fit a chosen GPU memory budget.
...
- ModelScope released EntroPack, an open-source PyTorch library for tuning AI model weight storage to fit a chosen GPU memory budget
- EntroPack lets developers adjust compression based on available GPU memory, trading accuracy for memory headroom on a sliding scale
- A model requiring 80 gigabytes of memory cannot load onto a card with 24 gigabytes unless its weights are compressed
- ModelScope has not published formal benchmarks comparing EntroPack with established compression libraries such as bitsandbytes or GPTQ

The project targets a persistent bottleneck in running large models, the limited memory on graphics processing units that forces teams to either buy more expensive hardware or shrink their models.

ModelScope, the open-model hub backed by Alibaba, described EntroPack in a post on its X account as offering flexible compression that lets users choose how aggressively to shrink weight storage.
...
A model that needs 80 gigabytes of memory will not load onto a card with 24 gigabytes unless its weights are compressed first.
...
Weight storage compression works by representing a model’s numerical parameters with fewer bits than the format they were trained in, trading some precision for a smaller memory footprint.
...
EntroPack’s pitch is flexibility rather than a single fixed compression ratio.

Instead of forcing every user into one aggressive quantization scheme, the library lets a developer dial compression up or down based on how much GPU memory they actually have available, trading accuracy for memory headroom on a sliding scale rather than an all-or-nothing switch.
...
GPU memory has become one of the defining cost pressures in AI deployment over the past two years, as model sizes have grown faster than the memory capacity of widely available hardware.

Nvidia‘s most capacious consumer and prosumer cards still top out well below what large open-weight models need natively, which has pushed an entire category of compression, quantization and offloading tools out of corporate labs and independent open-source contributors alike.
...
The broader open-weight ecosystem, including models from Alibaba’s own Qwen family and Meta‘s Llama line, has leaned heavily on compression research to keep its models runnable on consumer and mid-tier enterprise hardware rather than only data center silicon.
...
The practical test for EntroPack will be adoption among developers running open-weight models on constrained hardware, a group that has grown as open models have gotten larger and more capable.

Tools that let a 70-billion-parameter model run comfortably on a single consumer GPU rather than a multi-card server rack carry real cost implications, often the difference between a side project being feasible or not.

ModelScope has not published formal benchmarks comparing EntroPack against established compression libraries such as bitsandbytes or GPTQ, so independent testing will determine whether its flexible approach holds up against purpose-built fixed-ratio alternatives already in wide use.
